judge_notes.opus: J won by leading with one story and saying why it matters: Oracle's raise landed as 'investors are repricing how much AI infrastructure debt they will absorb,' backed by concrete credit signals. It barely edged K ('a reminder that AI capital spending is still outrunning investor comfort'), which has the same instinct but less depth and misfiles AWS numbers under 'In policy news.' B finished last because it is mostly disclaimers: 'explicitly not a production-ready product,' 'the incidents themselves are not dated,' 'rather than another model release.' Its lead is buried under caveats.
judge_notes.glm: I won with the clearest news judgment: Oracle's raise led with precise SEC filing detail and the $20 billion cap, then Pando and Abu Dhabi with concrete scale figures, all in clean prose. G followed closely, pairing the most distinctive story (FlashProve with tokens/sec and MB figures) with tightly written regulation and financing items. D and H lost for opposite failures: D buried concrete news under hedging caveats and vague abstractions, while H was so thin it read as a placeholder, capping its two stories with a 'should be read within their stated test conditions' disclaimer. L was undercut by process leakage ('verified before the cutoff') and C by an outright incomplete sentence ('deleted about 30,000 by mistake').
judge_notes.astra: I wins through active prose, specific outcomes and relatively disciplined selection, though its technical lead still needs trimming. L has the strongest financial interpretation but loses ground on its overloaded final sentence. K finishes last because the missing object after '30,000' makes an important claim incomplete, on top of persistent unrelated-story stacking.
judge_notes.grok: H is the only strong piece: named actors, hard numbers, no broken sentence. I, G, and F are the next tier — real stakes, then a list joint, an unnamed sector claim, or a soft middle. J has the best financing and policy paragraphs and is capped at 3 by a comma splice. B is clean ordinary wire. From L down, a unitless '30,000,' a cutoff note, or theme-speak without figures. E and D need a rewrite: empty caution, and copy that narrates the desk.
judge_notes.dsflash: E wins because it leads with the mechanism and the number in the same breath (0.016% of parameters, 7.9% to 48.1%) and keeps every paragraph to one idea; its only damage is framing words like "moved on security and infrastructure in parallel." I is nearly as good, with the cleanest causal chain in the file, but spends its second sentence on a scope caveat instead of another fact. C, L and K carry the most reporting but each ends in a three-item pile-up that makes the reader triage. G loses outright: no figures anywhere, an unnamed benchmark, and a sentence whose entire content is that the reader should be careful — 73 words that could be deleted without losing a fact.
